patient.chief_complaint: Admitted for altered mental status thought to be hepatic encephalopathy — EEG shows triphasic waves, team debates whether this is NCSE or metabolic encephalopathy
patient.hpi: A 74-year-old White male retired engineer with known alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C) was admitted for worsening confusion over 3 days. His wife reports he has been increasingly confused, sleeping most of the day, and having 'shaking of his hands' in the morning. He has a history of recurrent hepatic encephalopathy managed with lactulose and rifaximin. His gastroenterologist initiated a lactulose increase but he has not improved. He had no prior seizures. On examination he is confused, unable to state the date or year, with coarse asterixis. He has jaundice, spider angiomata, and caput medusae. Neurologically, he was thought to have typical hepatic encephalopathy and was admitted to the medicine floor. Neurology was called when nursing noted intermittent rhythmic limb movements not explained by asterixis. EEG was ordered. The electroencephalographer's read: 'Generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology — may represent hepatic encephalopathy (triphasic waves from metabolic cause) or NCSE. Expert consultation recommended.' The medical team is uncertain: should we give benzodiazepines for possible NCSE (risky in liver failure — may precipitate deeper hepatic coma) or should we observe and continue treating hepatic encephalopathy (risk of untreated NCSE if that is the diagnosis)?

eeg.impression: DIAGNOSTICALLY AMBIGUOUS. Classic triphasic wave morphology of hepatic encephalopathy PLUS superimposed periods of sharper 3-4 Hz activity that may represent NCSE. This is the classic clinical dilemma: triphasic waves vs NCSE. CRITICAL RISK ASSESSMENT: Benzodiazepines in severe hepatic encephalopathy can worsen hepatic coma and cause respiratory failure. SAFER APPROACH: IV levetiracetam (hepatically safe alternative) trial rather than benzodiazepine trial to assess EEG response without precipitating hepatic decompensation. Concomitantly: treat hepatic encephalopathy aggressively (ammonia reduction). Clinical correlation recommended.

ct.impression: Normal brain CT — hepatic encephalopathy does not show structural changes on CT. No hemorrhage. No structural precipitant for EEG changes. Metabolic/hepatic cause for EEG triphasic waves is the primary explanation.
recommended_actions: Aggressive HE treatment: D50 immediately, lactulose enemas, treat SBP with ceftriaxone
Diagnostic paracentesis for SBP already performed
Treat hyponatremia carefully (max 6-8 mEq/L in 24h in cirrhosis)

output.impression: The 3-4 Hz sharpened runs (previously ambiguous) resolved with ammonia correction — these were metabolic fluctuations of triphasic waves, not NCSE. Clinical improvement correlates. Diagnosis: hepatic encephalopathy-related EEG changes without primary NCSE. Left temporal epileptiform discharges persist — may represent chronic brain lesion requiring continued monitoring. Clinical correlation recommended.

interactions.description: Valproate is CONTRAINDICATED in hepatic failure — valproate causes hepatotoxicity and hyperammonemia via inhibiting urea cycle. In Child-Pugh C cirrhosis with already elevated ammonia, valproate would dramatically worsen HE and liver failure.
interactions.clinical_recommendation: NEVER use valproate in hepatic encephalopathy or liver failure. Use levetiracetam.

interactions.description: Benzodiazepines in cirrhosis: significantly prolonged half-life (reduced hepatic metabolism), accumulate to toxic levels, and precipitate/worsen hepatic encephalopathy by enhancing GABA-A receptor sensitivity. Even one standard dose of diazepam can cause prolonged hepatic coma.
interactions.clinical_recommendation: Avoid benzodiazepines in Child-Pugh B/C cirrhosis. If absolutely required for status epilepticus, use lowest effective dose with close monitoring. Prefer levetiracetam.

interactions.description: Levetiracetam in cirrhosis: minimally hepatically metabolized (<10% hepatic); primarily renally cleared. Safe in liver failure with minimal dose adjustment. Preferred AED in hepatic encephalopathy-associated NCSE.
interactions.clinical_recommendation: Levetiracetam is the AED of choice in hepatic failure/cirrhosis. Standard dose if renal function adequate; reduce if concurrent CKD.

interactions.description: Propranolol in hepatic encephalopathy: can worsen hepatic coma by reducing hepatic blood flow and impairing gluconeogenesis. Hold propranolol during acute decompensation.
interactions.clinical_recommendation: Hold propranolol during acute HE episode — can impair liver recovery and worsen hypoglycemia. Restart when clinically stable.

output.summary: Cirrhosis AED rules: levetiracetam = safe; valproate = CONTRAINDICATED (hepatotoxic, hyperammonemia); benzodiazepines = avoid (worsen HE). Also: hold propranolol during acute decompensation.

results.title: EEG in hepatic encephalopathy: triphasic waves versus NCSE
results.key_finding: Triphasic waves of HE and NCSE GPDs are morphologically similar and the distinction is clinically important. Key differentiators: (1) Ammonia level — markedly elevated favors HE; (2) Clinical response to metabolic correction — triphasic waves improve with ammonia normalization, NCSE does not; (3) EEG reactivity — triphasic waves show reactivity to stimulation; NCSE may not; (4) Benzodiazepine trial — dangerous in cirrhosis; levetiracetam preferred diagnostic test. Valproate and benzodiazepines are contraindicated in cirrhosis.

output.summary: Triphasic waves vs NCSE in cirrhosis: correct ammonia first; if EEG improves with HE treatment, diagnosis was metabolic. Levetiracetam (not benzodiazepines) for cautious AED trial. Valproate absolutely contraindicated in liver failure. Benzodiazepines worsen HE — avoid.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy (Child-Pugh C cirrhosis) with SBP-precipitated acute decompensation, EEG showing triphasic waves mimicking NCSE; resolved with ammonia correction; no primary NCSE

differential.key_features: EEG sharpened 3-4 Hz runs initially suggest possible NCSE; however resolution with ammonia correction confirms metabolic origin; left temporal epileptiform activity noted but not causing current presentation
Autoimmune panel negative; CSF normal; clear metabolic precipitant (SBP + elevated ammonia); triphasic waves not limbic encephalitis pattern
Last drink 3 years ago; not acute withdrawal; alcoholic cirrhosis does not cause withdrawal if abstinent for years

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Triphasic waves at 1.5-2 Hz with anterior phase lag — HE pattern; plus possible ictal sharpening

optimal_actions.action: Serum ammonia immediately — critical for HE vs NCSE differentiation
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia 186 µmol/L — markedly elevated, consistent with HE driving EEG changes

Diagnostic paracentesis for SBP workup — elevated WBC 12.4, clinician suspected SBP precipitant
Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily for SBP (E. coli) — treat the HE precipitant
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia improving as infection resolves; EEG triphasic waves improve

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Valproate = hepatotoxic + hyperammonemic; benzodiazepines = worsens HE; levetiracetam = safe

optimal_actions.action: IV levetiracetam 500 mg (reduced dose for liver/renal function) — cautious AED trial; do NOT use benzodiazepines
optimal_actions.expected_finding: EEG improvement correlates with ammonia correction (not isolated AED response)

optimal_actions.action: Repeat EEG at 24 hours after metabolic correction — if triphasic waves improve with ammonia normalization, diagnosis is HE not NCSE
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Triphasic waves improving at 24h with ammonia correction; sharpened 3-4 Hz runs resolved

critical_actions: IV dextrose immediately — hypoglycemia in liver failure is life-threatening
Ammonia level immediately — markedly elevated ammonia confirms HE
Diagnostic paracentesis and treat SBP — precipitant for HE decompensation
Valproate is absolutely CONTRAINDICATED — hepatotoxic and causes hyperammonemia in liver failure
Benzodiazepines are dangerous in cirrhosis — prolonged HE, respiratory failure; use levetiracetam
Hold propranolol during acute HE — impairs gluconeogenesis and hepatic blood flow
contraindicated_actions: Valproate for NCSE in cirrhosis — causes hyperammonemia and hepatotoxicity; would worsen both HE and liver failure
Benzodiazepines empirically for triphasic waves — worsen HE, cause prolonged sedation in liver failure
Treating EEG triphasic waves as NCSE without first correcting ammonia and metabolic derangements
Continuing propranolol during acute HE — worsens hypoglycemia and hepatic recovery
key_reasoning_points: Triphasic waves of hepatic encephalopathy vs NCSE GPDs: the KEY diagnostic approach is metabolic correction first — if EEG improves with ammonia correction, it was HE not NCSE
Valproate is absolutely contraindicated in liver failure — inhibits urea cycle enzymes causing further hyperammonemia (ammonia can rise dramatically), and is hepatotoxic
Benzodiazepines in cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B/C): prolonged half-life (reduced hepatic metabolism), accumulate, precipitate/deepen hepatic coma — levetiracetam is the safe AED
SBP is the most common precipitant of acute HE decompensation in cirrhotic patients — always perform diagnostic paracentesis when HE decompensates
Hypoglycemia in liver failure is common (impaired gluconeogenesis) and is itself a cause of EEG changes and seizures — give dextrose FIRST before any other assessment

red_herrings.data_point: EEG report: 'sharpening of triphasic waves at 3-4 Hz — possible NCSE'
red_herrings.intended_effect: Initiate benzodiazepines for suspected NCSE without metabolic workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Sharpening of triphasic waves in HE is a metabolic fluctuation, not true NCSE. Metabolic correction (ammonia normalization) resolves both the clinical and EEG changes. Benzodiazepines in cirrhosis are dangerous.

red_herrings.data_point: Rhythmic limb movements noted by nursing
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude NCSE based on rhythmic movements
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Rhythmic movements in HE can be myoclonic jerks or asterixis variants — not necessarily NCSE. EEG correlation is required. Metabolic correction first before AED treatment.

metadata.teaching_points: Triphasic waves vs NCSE in cirrhosis; valproate contraindicated in liver failure; benzodiazepines worsen HE; levetiracetam safe in cirrhosis; SBP as HE precipitant; hypoglycemia in liver failure
metadata.pitfalls: Valproate for NCSE in cirrhosis; benzodiazepines empirically; treating EEG changes without correcting ammonia; missing SBP precipitant; continuing propranolol in acute HE
metadata.clinical_pearl: Triphasic waves in cirrhosis: correct ammonia FIRST. Valproate = absolutely contraindicated (hyperammonemia + hepatotoxic). Benzodiazepines = dangerous (worsens HE). Levetiracetam = safe AED in liver failure.
